title: Species of large genera cluster unequally around certain species

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Species of large genera cluster unequally around certain species

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Species of large genera are not equally distinct from one another but are clustered in little groups around certain other species, as varieties are clustered around their parent species.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: As Fries has well remarked, little groups of species are generally clustered like satellites around certain other species.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter II, “Variation under Nature”; section “Many of the species of the larger genera resemble varieties in being very closely, but unequally, related to each other, and in having restricted ranges”. Scope: species within large genera

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch02-12: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public trees and sequences directly encode unequal relatedness among species. Several defensible clustering statistics can test the core assertion broadly, despite ambiguity about satellites.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Quantify imbalance and multimodality of within-genus phylogenetic or phenotypic distances in large genera against equal-dispersion null models. Recurrent tight subclusters around central or ancestral forms support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A 'central species' needs an explicit definition.

Taxonomic splitting itself creates clusters.

fields.value:

data existence: 0.91

operationalizability: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.73

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Trees and trait tables can show uneven spacing inside large genera for well-sampled groups. The specific picture of satellites around certain species is stricter than generic tree imbalance, and standard phylogenies often erase the paraphyly that picture needs. The analysis is feasible and only moderately discriminating once a branching null is included.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure clustering of species around a few centers inside large genera, using morphological nearest-neighbour structure or phylogenetic satellites around paraphyletic nominal species, and compare that clustering with a constant-rate branching null. Excess clustering around a few species would support the satellite pattern; distances as even as the null would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Satellite species around a still-living 'parent' require paraphyletic species concepts that many trees have already removed.

Ordinary branching processes already produce clusters, so the null has to be explicit.

Morphological clustering and phylogenetic clustering answer different versions of the statement.
